title: Brooklyn Comic Pooja Reddy Turns Kentucky Roots Into Country Cabaret
excerpt: Her one-woman show "Pooja Reddy is White Trash" at Joe's Pub uses stand-up and original country songs to explore a South Indian upbringing in rural Kentucky.
body:
• Pooja Reddy, a Brooklyn-based comedy writer and stand-up raised in a small Kentucky farming community, has premiered her one-woman country cabaret, "Pooja Reddy is White Trash," at Joe's Pub at The Public Theater in Manhattan.
  • The show — developed with director Neal Gupta and music director Emma Jayne — uses stand-up and original country songs as a love letter to the complex identities of Southerners, many of them immigrants and people of color.
  • Reddy's Kentucky childhood included hunting, fishing, and country music; her South Indian immigrant parents settled there because the town lacked doctors. The nearest Hindu temple was 90 miles away.
  • In New York? The show plays Joe's Pub (next date October 6), with more dates October 12 and 14 in Brooklyn; her September 22 NPR "All Things Considered" interview is free to stream.

She grew up hunting and fishing in rural Kentucky, learned Southern politeness and chewing tobacco "at a tender age," and went home every night to pappu, annam, and biryani. Now Brooklyn-based comedy writer and stand-up Pooja Reddy has turned that upbringing into "Pooja Reddy is White Trash," a one-woman country cabaret that premiered at Joe's Pub at The Public Theater in Manhattan this September — and is quietly becoming one of the most original Indian American stage voices of the year.

The show, developed with director Neal Gupta and music director Emma Jayne, mixes stand-up with original country songs. NPR, which featured Reddy on "All Things Considered" on September 22 in a segment reported by Nashville Public Radio's Jewly Hight, called it "a new country cabaret show that defies stereotypes." Reddy describes it as a love letter to the complex identities of Southerners — many of whom are immigrants and people of color.

A Kentucky childhood, a Hyderabad heritage

Reddy's parents, South Indian immigrants with roots in Hyderabad, settled in a small Kentucky farming community because the town lacked doctors — her father is a physician. The nearest Hindu temple was 90 miles away, and she socialized with friends at their Christian congregations. Her signature bit captures the cultural negotiation: begging her parents to let her attend a Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife sleepaway camp. "I'm convinced that the only reason they let me go is because it was called Camp Currie... They're like, finally, our daughter is showing an interest in cooking."

"It felt like I had a very normal, Southern upbringing just like any of my other classmates did. But at the end of the night, I was just going home, and I was eating pappu and annam and biryani and eating some South Indian food."

— Pooja Reddy

An unlikely résumé

Before comedy, Reddy worked in Washington, D.C. for First Lady Michelle Obama and then at the United Nations. She is a correspondent for PBS' ALL ARTS Network and Disney's Localish, was featured in the 2025 Emmy-nominated PBS special "Voices Rising," co-hosts the New York Times-recommended comedy show "Kutti Gang," and holds a spot in the Joe's Pub Working Group and The Public Theatre's New Work Development Artist Residency.

Her songs carry the show's sharpest writing. In "Wish You Were Here," she sings: "Y'all, I had an amazing childhood. They would have written books about it, like Chicken Soup for the Indian Girl's Soul, who was the only brown person in her school, and her classmates would call her Pooha 'cause they thought she was Mexican."

Identity, without the conflict

What distinguishes Reddy's act is its refusal of the standard immigrant-identity crisis. "I don't think I've ever been confused about my identity in terms of how Indian I am or how American I am. That's never been a conflict for me," she told NPR. Instead, the show's target is the assumption that a brown woman from Kentucky is a contradiction at all. "I've never met anyone from Kentucky," she jokes of coastal reactions. "It's probably because they're not smart enough to leave."

"We're not all that different. And maybe if somebody who looks like they wouldn't be a typical southerner, maybe if it's coming from me, then you might actually buy it and believe it."

— Pooja Reddy

Where to see her

"Pooja Reddy is White Trash" continues at Joe's Pub (tickets via publictheater.org), with upcoming dates including an October 12 reproductive-rights fundraiser at Littlefield in Brooklyn and an October 14 appearance with Aparna Nancherla at Union Hall. Her full schedule is at poojareddycomedy.com, and the NPR interview is free to stream.
